reason: Attacked on wording, locator, translation year, scope and form; it held on all of them. (1) WORDING. I fetched the Frechtman text at marxists.org/reference/subject/ethics/de-beauvoir/ambiguity/ch03.htm and had the sentence containing the phrase absurd vegetation returned in full. It comes back character for character as proposed, both semicolons in place, from the opening clause about perpetuating itself to the closing clause about limits the subject assigns himself. Nothing is spliced, nothing is trimmed, and the sentence is a whole sentence. (2) TRANSLATION DRIFT, which is this track's usual killer, is the one thing that cannot be hidden here: the page read IS the named translation, not a summary of it or another hand's rendering. (3) LOCATOR. The same fetch returned the chapter's own list of section headings, in order: 1 The Aesthetic Attitude, 2 Freedom and Liberation, 3 The Antinomies of Action, 4 The Present and the Future, 5 Ambiguity. The sentence falls in section 2, Freedom and Liberation, of Part III, whose full title is The Positive Aspect of Ambiguity. The source line's Part III, 2, Freedom and Liberation is therefore right, and it is not an assertion but a reading. (4) TRANSLATION YEAR, the point I expected to break it on. The Marxists Internet Archive header for this text credits Frechtman but dates it First Published: in 1949 by Citadel Press, which would make the source line's 1948 wrong. It does not. Open Library carries a Philosophical Library record titled The Ethics of Ambiguity, 1948, and the trade listings for the first English edition agree: New York, Philosophical Library, 1948, translated from the French by Bernard Frechtman, 161 pages, one year after the 1947 Gallimard original, Beauvoir's first book in English. Citadel Press is the reprint house, from 1949 onward, and carries the same Frechtman text, which is what the evidence field already says. The named year is the year of the published translation whose wording the line uses, as the rule requires. (5) ATTRIBUTION AND SPEAKER. Beauvoir's own expository prose, first person plural nowhere, no character speaking, so there is no speaker to name and no reporter trap. The line appears on none of the brief's misattribution rows. (6) shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Beauvoir at 1 of 3 for the year (month 1), not banned. I checked the April verdict list for a second Beauvoir and there is none, so the no-person-twice-in-the-month rule is safe. (7) FORM. Source line leads with the name, 113 characters, no dash of any kind, no straight double quote; the quotation is unbroken prose and ends in a full stop; Philosophy is the right tag for The Ethics of Ambiguity in the closed vocabulary; first published 1947 and 1948, so pre-1999, and it is none of scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory; nothing here would need a content warning. ONE NOTE, not a refutation. At 383 characters it would be the second longest quotation in the year, a shade under March's Nietzsche at 386, and it earns that length only if the reader gets to the third clause. The editor may want to say so rather than discover it on the card.
